    1. Executive Summary
Sudan continues to face a multitude of complex challenges as it grapples with the impacts of prolonged
conflict and crisis. Years of political instability, economic decline, and humanitarian emergencies —
exacerbated by the impacts of climate change — have significantly disrupted and even reversed many
development gains.

An outbreak of conflict in April 2023 has fragmented the country, resulted in serious human rights violations
and abuses against civilians, and exacerbated many of the country’s existing challenges with a profound
impact on the society, economy, and environment. Vulnerable groups, including women, children, young
people, displacement affected populations, persons with disabilities, and conflict affected communities,
have been disproportionately impacted.

While the emphasis remains on delivering emergency life-saving and -sustaining humanitarian assistance,
there is a growing recognition of the urgent need for recovery and resilience building. As such, this Interim
UN Cooperation Framework 2026–2028 (ICF) represents the UN’s collective contribution toward a pivot to
recovery, resiliency, and peace efforts, as well a reaffirmation of its longstanding relationship with Sudan
and its people.

The ICF covers a shorter timeframe than would be the case in a more traditional development context given
Sudan’s complex and fluid environment which poses challenges to longer term planning. Its development
was informed by a comprehensive analysis of the situation in the country through the lens of the SDGs, as
well as lessons learned exercises of previous UN frameworks. Extensive consultations with national
authorities, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), civil society organizations (CSOs) — including
women- and youth-led groups — international development partners, and other stakeholders were also
instrumental in the design of the ICF. Cumulatively, this process resulted in the identification of four
Strategic Priorities against which the ICF is structured, specifically:

   1.   Restoration of inclusive essential services
   2.   Socioeconomic recovery, resilient livelihoods, and food security
   3.   Peace, justice, and strong institutions
   4.   Environment, climate action, and disaster resilience

Recognising the chronic, multifaceted, and overlapping challenges facing Sudan, the ICF seeks to reflect
the complementary and mutually reinforcing nature of the solutions required to tackle the country’s
multidimensional challenges. This includes the imperative for the UN to apply a humanitarian-development-
peace nexus approach throughout the design, coordination, and implementation of its activities in support
of this ICF to contribute to the protection of human rights and reduce vulnerabilities. To this end,
interventions will prioritize community-level area-based approaches. While the ICF is country-wide in
scope, it is also important to recognise the limited or lack of UN presence across large parts of Sudan,
particularly in Rapid Support Forces (RSF) controlled areas, that will pose significant challenges to
implementation in these areas.




                                                     5
 While the variety of challenges that Sudan continues to face should not be underestimated, the UN, through
this ICF, remains committed to supporting the country and its people in its efforts towards a more peaceful,
resilient, equal, prosperous, and sustainable future for all, particularly the most vulnerable.

    2. Progress Towards the 2030 Agenda
           2.1       Country Context
Since its independence in 1956, Sudan has been beset with recurring political, governance, and security
instability, including 19 successful or attempted military coups, internal conflicts, authoritarian rule, and
natural disasters resulting in protracted humanitarian crises which have impacted generations of Sudanese
and hindered progress towards inclusive and sustainable development. The outbreak of conflict in April
2023 has resulted in serious human rights violations and abuses against civilians and exacerbated many of
the country’s existing challenges with a profound impact on the society, economy, and environment. While
the Port Sudan-based Government’s 2025 ‘Roadmap for Peace’ outlines a process for a transition to a
civilian-led government and national elections through the resumption of an inclusive all-Sudanese political
dialogue, the subsequent establishment of a parallel RSF-led administration (not recognized by the
international community) have further complicated peace efforts.

Sudan is facing the world’s largest humanitarian, protection, displacement, and hunger crisis. Tens of
thousands of Sudanese have lost their lives or have incurred disabilities due to severe injuries, while 30.4
million people are in need of humanitarian assistance in 2025.1 Extreme poverty has increased sharply, with
the proportion of the population living on less than US$ 2.15 per day increasing from an estimated 30 per
cent in 2022 to 57 per cent in 2024.2 Over the medium term, extreme poverty is expected to remain high at
64 per cent.3

Half the population remain food insecure, with nearly 24.6 million people facing acute food insecurity as of
December 2024. Famine conditions were determined to be in place between October to November 2024 in
Zamzam, Abu Shouk, and Al Salam camps in North Darfur, as well as in the Western Nuba Mountains,
affecting residents, IDPs, and refugees. Famine was projected to continue in the same areas between
December 2024 and May 2025 while expanding in localities in the North Darfur state, estimated to affect a
total of 637,234 people.4

An estimated 64 per cent of female-headed households in 10 states are food insecure (of whom 14 per cent
are experiencing severe levels of food insecurity) compared to 48 per cent of male-headed households (of
whom 7 per cent are severely food insecure).5 Eighty-four per cent of women in Sudan are unable to meet
the minimum acceptable diet, a 5 per cent increase over 2023.6 Sudan also ranks among the top four

The health system has largely collapsed, with 70–80 per cent of hospitals in conflict-affected states non-
functional, leaving 11 million people without essential medical services, including sexual, reproductive,
maternal, and child care.8,9 Moreover, only 60 per cent of health facilities nationwide were reported as either
partially or fully functional in July 2025.10 The worsening water and sanitation crisis has left nearly 15 million
people without access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation.11 More than 17 million out-of-school
children are at risk of never returning to learning, with an estimated 2.5 million girls (representing 74 per cent
of girls of school-going age) not attending school.12

Sudan’s economy contracted by more than 20.1 per cent in 2023 and 20.3 per cent in 2024. 13,14 The
Government has lost a large share of its revenue base, severely impacting its ability to provide public
services. Triple-digit inflation rates (averaging 177 per cent in 202415) and the devaluation of the Sudanese
currency (300 per cent since the start of the war16) further strain the ability of households to meet their basic
needs. Such hardships have resulted in families and children resorting to negative coping mechanisms,
including children's engagement in the worst forms of child labour.

The continuing conflict has also led to large parts of the country, including many urban centres, to be heavily
contaminated with explosive hazards, threating lives and livelihoods, restricting access to homes and services, and
impeding broader recovery efforts.

Sudan remains particularly susceptible to the impact of climate change and environmental disasters,
primarily floods and drought, which exacerbate existing vulnerabilities and increase the risk of inter-
communal violence and humanitarian needs. Conflict-related environmental damage, including from
explosive hazards and war debris, will also continue to pose a threat far into the future.

           2.2       Leave no one Behind
Inequalities in Sudan are longstanding, entrenched and based on multiple and often interrelated and
overlapping factors, including economic, social, and political factors. Of the 30.4 million people in need of
humanitarian assistance in 2025, 24.4 per cent are women, 51.4 per cent are children, 5.3 per cent are older
people, and 15 per cent are persons with disability. 17

The ongoing changing conflict dynamics have disproportionately affected women and girls, further
exacerbating their vulnerability to violence, displacement, discrimination, poverty, and economic

Children are exposed to multiple rights violations including child recruitment, sexual violence, abduction
and trafficking, child marriage, child labour, GBV, and separation from families. With millions of children not
in school, girls and boys are at further risk of abuse and exploitation by armed groups and traffickers.
Accounting for 41 per cent of the population, young people (aged 15-24 years) lack job opportunities and
services and face additional protection threats such as mobilization by armed groups.22

Over 11 million people (female 54 per cent; male 46 per cent) — well over half of whom are children — have
been displaced.23 Displaced populations have lost their livelihoods, properties, jobs, and dignity. There are
over 859,000 refugees in Sudan who have been equally impacted by the war. The sudden and large influx of
IDPs has placed a significant strain on existing urban services and infrastructure, resulting in increased
tensions between IDPs and host communities. Sudan has also been a major host of refugees and asylum
seekers, estimated at 1.14 million in March 2023, with the projected number for 2025 standing at 892,000.24

Fifteen per cent of those in need of humanitarian assistance in 2025 are persons with disabilities,
representing 4.7 million people.25 Persons with disabilities are disproportionately affected, often left behind
and insufficiently protected in emergencies and struggle to access humanitarian assistance and protection
due to institutional, attitudinal, environmental, and communication barriers.

Rural communities face multiple vulnerabilities, including limited access to essential services and fragile
livelihoods driven by war and climate change impacts.

      3. United Nations Support to the 2030 Agenda
            3.1       From a UN Country Analysis to ICF Priorities
To ensure that the new ICF would be as informed and evidence based as possible, the UN system in Sudan
undertook a comprehensive and multidimensional analysis of the situation in Sudan through the framework
of the SDGs to assess progress against the Goals. The UN also undertook an internal lesson learned exercise
on the expired United Nations Development Assistance Framework 2018–2021 (UNDAF) and expiring UN
Common Approach 2024–2025 to draw on past experiences to inform the formulation of this ICF.

The formulation of the new ICF was undertaken in close collaboration with the national partners. A
dedicated ‘Joint Task Team’ provided technical oversight and coordination between the UN and Government
partners throughout the ICF development process. Additional technical consultations were undertaken with
relevant line ministries and other national entities to inform UN sectoral interventions. The UN undertook
wide ranging consultations with various other stakeholders, including international and national NGOs,
CSOs, private sector entities, and international development partners, amongst others.

Cumulatively, this process resulted in the identification of four complementary and mutually reinforcing
Strategic Priorities against which to structure the ICF (note: the numbering of the Strategic Priorities does
not denote any hierarchy of importance), specifically:

     1.    Restoration of inclusive essential services
     2.    Socioeconomic recovery, resilient livelihoods, and food security
     3.    Peace, justice, and strong institutions
     4.    Environment, climate action, and disaster resilience

These Strategic Priorities were informed by and are aligned to the Government of Sudan’s ‘Economic Vision
for the Post-war period, Reconstruction, and Compensation 2025–2028’. Furthermore, the Priorities also
reflect the UN’s ‘Six Transitions’ and four ‘Engine Room Actions’.26 Implementation of the ICF will be
underpinned by the UN system-wide priority on protection from sexual exploitation and abuse (see Box 1
below).




26
  Anchored in the SDGs, the ‘Six Transitions’ have been identified by the UN system globally as transformative entry points that can have catalytic and
multiplier effects across the Goals and an outsized determinant impact for their achievement. These are: 1) Food systems; 2) Energy access and affordability;
3) Digital Connectivity; 4) Education; 5) Jobs and social protection; and 6) Climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution.
Additionally, UNCTs and UN Resident Coordinators will enable and deliver four 'engine room' actions at the country level that 1) Drive the shifts across policy
and regulatory frameworks, going beyond the standard sectoral approaches; 2) Facilitate the identification and development of pipelines of bankable and
market-ready national projects with participation of both public and private sectors, including by providing access to world-class expertise; 3) Convene all
relevant actors to attract the needed financing from all sources to help develop the ‘deal room’ – a financing mix with innovative instruments – for each of
the transitions; and 4) Commit to capacity-building at scale to support public institutions and civil society in this process, ensuring a steady increase in
capacities over time to reinforce and sustain these investments.

  Box 1: Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse

 Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) is a key priority for the UNCT entities, with a special
 focus on prioritizing victims' rights and creating an environment in which sexual exploitation and abuse
 (SEA) do not occur. SEA is unacceptable behaviour and is prohibited for UN personnel and UN
 implementing partners. The UNCT entities will therefore pursue all appropriate means to protect against,
 prevent and respond to SEA, and will require a similar commitment from its partners.

 In delivering on the obligations articulated in the present Interim Cooperation Framework, the UNCT and
 the Government of Sudan affirm their commitment to preventing and responding to reports of SEA in
 connection with their personnel involved in common/joint projects. It is understood that this would entail
 the need to: (i) adhere to common values on PSEA, (ii) take preventative measures against SEA, (iii)
 investigate allegations, and (iv) take appropriate corrective action when incidents occur, including
 providing support to victims in accordance with a victim-centred approach.

to and reinforcing those in others (see Figure 1: Intersections and complementarities across ICF outputs areas).

  3.3 Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus Oriented Approaches

throughout the design, coordination, and implementation of its activities in support of this ICF. (see Section 4.2

humanitarian and development coordination structures to identify complementarities between recovery
and resilience-building approaches and those undertaken through humanitarian frameworks, particularly
Humanitarian Needs and Response Plans (HNRPs), to inform future programming.

     Box 2: Durable Solutions to Displacement

     Addressing Sudan’s displacement crisis demands a bold, coordinated, and forward-looking response anchored
     firmly in the humanitarian-development-peace nexus. As such, solutions to displacement must be rooted in
     comprehensive interventions that span all ICF priorities. This includes ensuring inclusive and equitable access to
     essential services, establishing safe and protective environments, expanding economic and livelihood
     opportunities, mitigating environmental and disaster risks, and fostering social cohesion, stability, and peace.
     Tailored approaches are needed to address the intersecting vulnerabilities of displacement-affected populations.
     Investing in durable solutions also aligns with Sudan’s national priorities, international commitments under the
     Global Compact on Refugees (2018), the UN Secretary General’s Action Agenda on International Displacement
     (2022), and the 2030 Agenda.

     To this end, the multi-stakeholder Durable Solutions Working Group aims to improve coordination across durable
     solutions-related partners, promote collective approaches with partners at all levels, and ensure solutions-focused
     programming remains principled, coherent, and well-coordinated, while integrating whole-of-displacement and
     area-based approaches.27

the Status of Refugees (1951); the IASC Framework on Durable Solutions for Internally Displaced Persons (2010); the Global Compact on Refugees (2018);
and the IASC Policy on Protection of Internally Displaced Persons (2024).

         3.4    Cooperation Framework Priorities and Outcomes
           Strategic Priority 1: Restoration of Inclusive Essential Services
Outcome 1: By 2028, more people across Sudan — particularly groups in vulnerable situations —
have improved access to functional, inclusive, equitable, integrated, quality, safe, and sustainable
essential services that enhance their well-being and resilience.

                                  UN support to Outcome achievement

Health Services: The UN will support efforts towards equitable access to essential health services through
Sudan’s Universal Health Coverage Priority Benefits Package, focusing on policy reform, infrastructure,
skilled human resources, sustainable financing, and stronger coordination. Contributions will be made to
strengthening digital health solutions to enhance quality, efficiency, and transparency. The UN will also
contribute to efforts for equitable workforce distribution, essential medicines, and addressing antimicrobial
resistance via the National Action Plan under a One Health approach. Support will endeavour to expand
immunization, sexual and reproductive health, GBV clinical management, mental health, disease
prevention, vector control, health promotion, community-based care, and emergency response including
MISP. Cross-sectoral collaboration will contribute towards addressing broader health determinants.

Nutrition Services, Diets, and Practices: Alongside humanitarian response, the UN will contribute to the
expansion of preventive nutrition services, including infant and young child feeding, micronutrient support,
and growth monitoring. The UN will also support efforts to integrate treatment and supplementation for
acute malnutrition into facility and community health systems. Strengthened information and surveillance
systems will contribute towards improved service delivery and policymaking. The UN will also endeavour to
work with communities to promote healthy diets, create demand for services, and support nutrition-
sensitive practices. Through Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN), partnerships with national and sub-national
institutions, the private sector, UN agencies, NGOs, and civil society will be reinforced to mobilize resources
and advocacy for greater nutrition programming and support.

Inclusive, Accessible Education: The UN will work to promote equitable access to quality education for
all children — especially girls, refugees, displaced children, those with disabilities, and the out-of-school —
through support for governance, planning, policy development, evidence use, financing, and advocacy
aligned with the Transitional Education Plan 2025–2027. Where needed and funded, the UN will contribute
to the construction and rehabilitation of education facilities. Efforts will be undertaken to institutionalize
skills development, with the aim to boost girls’ enrolment, retention, completion, and access to Second
Chance Education. School feeding, nutrition-sensitive programming, and integrated WASH will improve
learning environments and outcomes. The UN will also aim to support digital platforms that expand access
to teaching and training, supporting holistic child development and lifelong learning opportunities.

Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene: The UN will endeavour to strengthen WASH systems through inclusive
coordination forums, policy development, institutional capacity-building, localization of supplies, and
evidence-based monitoring. Initiatives will focus on expanding access to WASH services via construction,

 rehabilitation, and upgrading of water facilities, latrines, service points, and medical waste management.
Conflict-resilient water and energy design norms and standards will be promoted, alongside gender-
responsive community participation in water management. The UN will also contribute to the scaling of
water-related loss and damage assessments to guide recovery planning and financing.

Protection Services: The UN will aim to strengthen prevention, mitigation, and response to protection
concerns by improving survivor-centred case management and referral to specialized services. Work will be
undertaken to enhance data and information systems to support evidence-based programming and
coordination. The UN will contribute to GBV prevention and response, including addressing harmful
practices such as female genital mutilation and child marriage, through community engagement, essential
services, temporary safe spaces, and stronger accountability mechanisms. Contributions will also be made
to the development of standard operating procedures and strengthening of frontline staff capacities to
improve service provision. The UN will also work to bolster national mine action capabilities — including
awareness raising, support to victims, and survey and clearance of explosive hazards — to enhance
community safety in areas impacted by explosive remnants of war.



              Strategic Priority 2: Socioeconomic Recovery, Resilient
                           Livelihoods, and Food Security
Outcome 2: By 2028, more people across Sudan — particularly groups in vulnerable situations —
benefit from inclusive economic opportunities, sustainable jobs and resilient livelihoods, and
improved food security.
                            UN support to Outcome achievement

Sustainable socioeconomic recovery and resilient livelihoods: The UN will contribute to the
strengthening of national and sub-national institutions to advance inclusive, gender-responsive economic
governance, budgetary planning, and policy development that enables private sector-led recovery. Efforts
will include implementation of the Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF) and fostering MSMEs,
particularly women- and youth-led enterprises, through improved infrastructure, innovative financing, and
sustainable job creation. The UN will endeavour to promote public-private partnerships to expand skills
development and access to digital infrastructure, agricultural insurance, cultural and creative economies,
and markets. Efforts will also seek to address discriminatory policies and practices, advancing women’s
economic participation through targeted employability initiatives, including in green and sustainable
economy sectors.

Resilient Agrifood Systems: The UN will aim to support agrifood system recovery by contributing towards
the building of food reserves, improving access to inputs, strengthening seed and forest systems, and
enhancing veterinary services, vaccine supply chains, and technology transfer. Infrastructure rehabilitation,
stronger value chains, circular economy practices, and better post-harvest management will be prioritized.
The UN will contribute to the revitalization of agricultural extension with gender-sensitive approaches, as
well as strengthening institutional capacity in food security, fisheries, livestock, and agriculture. The UN will

 also endeavour to promote gender-responsive, climate-smart, and conflict-sensitive practices.
Contributions will also be made to strengthening cooperatives and producer associations, including
women- and youth-led groups, to expand markets, local procurement, and compliance with standards,
while advancing pro-poor fiscal policies and financing.

Social Protection Systems: The UN will endeavour to promote shock-responsive, adaptable, and scalable
social protection systems with gender-responsive, resilience-building measures to help individuals,
communities, and institutions withstand and recover from shocks. Support will aim to include strengthening
data collection and analysis to inform system design, and building institutional capacity to coordinate,
finance, and monitor programmes effectively. Efforts will be made to link social protection to economic
recovery through enterprise development, innovative financing, and digital financial services, improving
livelihoods of vulnerable groups, including IDPs and refugees. With partners, the UN will also aim to expand
access to financial services for disadvantaged populations to reduce inequalities and enhance
socioeconomic resilience across communities.



              Strategic Priority 3: Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions
Outcome 3: By 2028, more people across Sudan — particularly groups in vulnerable situations — live
in a safer and more peaceful society with strengthened human rights protections, inclusive
institutions, and equitable access to justice.

                                  UN support to Outcome achievement

Inclusive Institutions, Community Structures, and Legal and Policy Frameworks: The UN will
endeavour to strengthen national and sub-national institutions to be more inclusive, gender-responsive, and
accountable. Support will aim to focus on institutional, legislative, and policy reforms at all levels, alongside
ratification of international human rights instruments to align with global standards. The UN will contribute
to the strengthening of community structures to advance participation in decision-making and act as agents
of resilience against violence and division. Efforts will aim to advance digital transformation and inclusion
and e-governance to improve efficiency, transparency, and service delivery, including stronger data
systems. Access to information and evidence generation and use will be prioritized to inform planning and
decision-making.

Rule of Law and Access to Justice: The UN will aim to contribute to the strengthening of justice, rule of
law, and human rights by supporting formal and traditional systems, accountability mechanisms, and
remedies for victims, including survivors of GBV and conflict-related sexual violence. Efforts will be
undertaken to reinforce the capacities of law enforcement and judicial institutions to uphold international
norms, with focus on child protection, non-refoulement, minimum age of criminal responsibility, and
alternatives to detention. Support will also be extended to enhance criminal justice responses to organized
crime and to strengthen forensic and investigative capacities. The UN will aim to enhance oversight of
Alternative Dispute Resolution and border management to seek to address trafficking and smuggling and
strengthening transnational cooperation to disrupt criminal networks. Work will be undertaken to reinforce

Outcome 4: By 2028, more people across Sudan — particularly groups in vulnerable situations —

Climate change and disaster risk resilience: The UN will aim to support the review and implementation
of climate change and disaster risk reduction policies and frameworks, including the Sendai Framework,
National Adaptation Plans (NAPs), and Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). It will endeavour to
facilitate access to international climate and disaster financing while strengthening institutional capacities
for inclusive, gender-responsive adaptation, mitigation, and risk management. Support will aim to cover
planning, budgeting, preparedness, response, and recovery. The UN will also contribute to the
enhancement of weather forecasting, multi-hazard early warning, and climate advisory services, promoting
coordinated systems and “early warning, early action” in line with the Early Warning for All (EW4All) initiative.

Environmental Protection, Recovery, and Sustainable Natural Resource Management: The UN will
work to strengthen environmental governance by contributing to the enhancement of institutional
capacities, advancing laws and policies on protection, recovery, and natural resource management, and
supporting adoption of Multilateral Environmental Agreements. Technical assistance will endeavour to
improve monitoring, evidence generation, and policymaking. The UN will assist in the capacity strengthening
of institutions, communities, and stakeholders at all levels to manage resources, heritage, and protected
areas in line with global standards, including the climate–peace–security nexus. Priorities will include

 combating desertification, restoring degraded zones, safeguarding ecosystems and biodiversity, and
promoting nature-based solutions. The UN will also aim to facilitate innovative financing for sustainable land
use, eco-friendly industries, and tourism.

strengthening of the capacities of institutions, communities, and the private sector to advance gender-
responsive renewable energy. Assistance will include technical support, regulatory and financing reforms,

energy access. Efforts will be undertaken to aid in the expansion of decentralized renewable energy to drive

    4.3     Resourcing the UN Interim Cooperation Framework
The UN in Sudan assessed the financial and other resources required to translate its ambitions into
implementable activities and actions. This included the formulation of a comprehensive Funding Framework
which assesses the amount, type, source, duration, and sequence of financial resources that are required,
available, and projected to be available, as well as those to be mobilized.

The UN will also endeavour to increase joint resource mobilization, financing, and programming as part of
its efforts to improve internal coherence and cost effectiveness. At the core of this effort is the Sudan Multi-
Partner Trust Fund (MPTF) which plays a pivotal role in fostering joint planning, resource pooling, and
coordinated implementation. The MPTF will also complement other pooled funding instruments such as the
UN Peacebuilding Fund and Joint SDG Fund.

The UN further plans to develop a joint resource mobilization strategy for the ICF. The UN Resident and
Humanitarian Coordinator will also support joint resource mobilization initiatives while UN entities will keep
the UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator informed of their resource mobilization efforts.

            Interim Cooperation Framework

 All UN entities — both resident and non-resident — implementing in Sudan in support of the ICF will derive
their respective country planning and programming instruments directly from this Framework, including the
verbatim integration of ICF outcomes into their documents. The UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator
will evaluate UN entity country programming instruments to validate their alignment with the ICF. UN entities
required to submit programme documents to their governing bodies will solicit review and endorsement by
the UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator prior to submission. To ensure maximum coherence across
the UN’s planning and programming landscape in Sudan, UN entities, to the extent possible, will also
endeavour to align the timelines of their country programming instruments with that of the ICF.

    4.5     Joint Workplans
The ICF is operationalized through joint workplans. All resident and non-resident UN entities implementing in
Sudan will contribute to the development of multi-agency output-level joint workplans through the Results Groups
in conjunction with other relevant UN coordination mechanisms. Joint workplans will reflect sub-outputs or
activities — to be implemented by either individual or multiple UN entities — that contribute to the realization of
ICF-level outputs. Workplans will be collated and reviewed in consultation with relevant national partners and
other external stakeholders, including through appropriate sectoral coordination mechanisms as appropriate.
Joint workplans will be reviewed, maintained, and updated on a periodic basis by the Results Groups and the Joint
Steering Committee to ensure they respond to the evolving country context and needs. Joint workplans will be
reflected within the online UNINFO platform to facilitate increased transparency and accountability, as well as
collective monitoring and reporting against ICF commitments.

    4.6     Business Operations Strategy in support of the UN Interim
            Cooperation Framework
The UN Sudan’s Operations Strategy 2.0 (BOS 2.0) provides the UNCT and OMT with a guiding framework to
elaborate strategic and cost-effective initiatives for linking business operations with programmatic needs
and requirements under the ICF. Underpinned by the principles of mutual recognition, client satisfaction,
and cost effectiveness, the BOS 2.0 aims to reduce duplication, leverage the common bargaining power of
the UN, maximize economies of scale, and reduce transaction costs across its common service lines. These
include administration, human resources, premises and facilities, finance services, information and
communication technology, logistics, and procurement. While the UN in Sudan has been exempted from
BOS implementation due to the impacts of the conflict and its associated complexities on UN operations, it
is expected to resume in the first year of ICF implementation and/or once conditions permit.

Key cross-cutting risk factors:

   •   Conflict and Insecurity: Persistently high and widespread conflict severely restricts access to populations, disrupts markets, and
       undermines governance and justice mechanisms. Conflict sensitivity and adaptive programming are essential.
   •   Institutional Fragility: Weak capacities and fragmentation at national and sub-national levels impede effective service delivery, economic
       governance, and human rights protection.
